question.text: Evaluate the repeated integral $\displaystyle \int_0^{\pi/4} \int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/4} \dfrac 1 {\sin^2 x \cos^2 y}\, \textrm d x \, \textrm dy .$
question.explanation:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int_0^{\pi/4} \left[\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/4} \dfrac 1 {\sin^2 x \cos^2 y}\, \textrm d x \right] \textrm dy & =\int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{1}{ \cos^2 y}\left[\int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/4} \dfrac 1 {\sin^2 x }\, \textrm d x \right] \textrm dy\\[5pt] & = \int_0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{1}{ \cos^2 y}\Big[-\cot x \Big]_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/4} \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{1}{ \cos^2 y}\left( -\cot \dfrac {3\pi}{4} + \cot \dfrac \pi 2 \right) \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _0^{\pi/4} \dfrac{1}{ \cos^2 y}\left( -(-1) + 0 \right) \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _0^{\pi/4} \dfrac {1} { \cos^2 y} \, \textrm dy \end{align}

Then, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int _0^{\pi/4} \dfrac {1} { \cos^2 y} \, \textrm dy &= \int _0^{\pi/4} \sec^2 y \, \textrm dy\\[5pt] & = \Big[ \tan y \Big]_{0}^{\pi/4} \\[5pt] & = \tan \dfrac \pi 4 - \tan 0 \\[5pt] & = 1-0 \\[5pt] & = 1 \end{align}

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant.

Making a substitution $x+y=u,$ $\textrm dx = \textrm du,$ we get.

\begin{align} \int _1^2 \int_{0}^1 \dfrac{1}{(x+y)^2}\, \textrm d x \textrm dy & =\int _1^2 \left[ \int_{0}^1 \dfrac{1}{(x+y)^2}\, \textrm d x \right] \textrm dy\\[5pt] & =\int _1^2 \left[ \int_{y}^{1+y} \dfrac{1}{u^2}\, \textrm d u \right] \textrm dy\\[5pt] & = \int_1^2 \left[ -\dfrac {1}{u} \right]_{y}^{1+y} \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _1^2 \left( -\dfrac {1}{y+1} + \dfrac {1}y \right)\, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_1^2 \left[\dfrac{1}{y} - \dfrac{1}{y+1} \right]\, \textrm dy \end{align}

Then, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int_1^2 \left[\dfrac{1}{y} - \dfrac{1}{y+1} \right]\, \textrm dy & = \big[ \ln{y} - \ln(y+1) \big]_1^2\\[5pt] &= \ln \left(\dfrac{y}{y+1} \right) \Bigg|_1^2\\[5pt] & = \ln \left( \dfrac{2}{3}\right)- \ln\left( \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\[5pt] & = \ln \left( \dfrac{2}{3}\right) + \ln\left( 2\right)\\[5pt] & = \ln \left( \dfrac{2}{3}\cdot 2\right) \\[5pt] &= \ln \left(\dfrac{4}{3} \right) \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the repeated integral $\displaystyle \int_{-2}^{-1} \int_{0}^{\sqrt 3} \dfrac 1 {y^2 (1+x^2)}\, \textrm d x \, \textrm dy. $
question.explanation:
First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int_{-2}^{-1} \left[\int_{0}^{\sqrt 3} \dfrac 1 {y^2 (1+x^2)}\, \textrm d x \right] \textrm dy & =\int_{-2}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{y^2} \left[\int_{0}^{\sqrt 3} \dfrac{1} {(1+x^2)}\, \textrm d x \right] \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{-2}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{y^2}\Big[\arctan x\Big]_{0}^{\sqrt 3} \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _{-2}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{y^2}\left(\arctan \sqrt 3 - \arctan 0 \right) \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _{-2}^{-1} \dfrac{1}{y^2}\left( \dfrac \pi 3 - 0 \right) \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _{-2}^{-1} \dfrac {\pi } {3y^2} \, \textrm dy\\[5pt] \end{align}

Then, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int _{-2}^{-1} \dfrac {\pi } {3y^2} \, \textrm dy & = \left[ -\dfrac {\pi} {3y} \right]_{-2}^{-1} \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac {\pi} {3\cdot (-1)} - \left(-\dfrac {\pi} {3\cdot (-2)}\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\pi} {3} - \dfrac {\pi} {6} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\pi} {6} \end{align}

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int_0^{\pi/2} \left[\int_{\pi}^{7\pi/6} \cos (2x+y)\, \textrm d x \right] \textrm dy & = \int_0^{\pi/2} \left[ \dfrac {1}2 \sin (2x+y) \right]_{\pi}^{7\pi/6} \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {1}2 \int _0^{\pi/2} \left(\sin \left(\dfrac {7\pi}3+y\right) - \sin (2\pi+y) \right) \textrm dy %& = \dfrac {1}2 \int _0^{\pi/2} \left(\sin \left(\dfrac {\pi} 3+y\right) - \sin y \right) \textrm dy \end{align}

Then, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} %\dfrac {1}2 \int _0^{\pi/2} \left(\sin \left(\dfrac {\pi} 3+y\right) - \sin y \right) \textrm dy \dfrac {1}2 & \int _0^{\pi/2} \left(\sin \left(\dfrac {7\pi}3+y\right) - \sin (2\pi+y) \right) \textrm dy \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}2 \left[-\cos \left(\dfrac {7\pi} 3+y\right) + \cos(2\pi + y) \right]_0^{\pi/2}\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {1}2 \left[-\cos \left(\dfrac {7\pi} 3+\dfrac {\pi}2\right) + \cos \left(\dfrac {7\pi} 3+0\right) + \cos \left(2\pi +\dfrac {\pi}2\right) - \cos (2\pi + 0) \right] \\[5pt] & = \dfrac {1}2 \left[ -\cos \left(\dfrac {17\pi}6\right) + \cos \left(\dfrac {7\pi}3\right) + \cos \left(\dfrac {5\pi}2\right) - \cos (2\pi) \right]\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {1}2 \left[ \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2} + \dfrac{1}{2} + 0 -1\right]\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {\sqrt 3 - 1} {4 } \end{align}

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int_{0}^{1} \left[ \int_{2}^{4} x^3y^2 \, \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d} y & =\int_{0}^{1} y^2 \left[ \int_{2}^{4} x^3 \, \textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d} y \\[5pt] & = \int_0^1 y^2 \left[ \dfrac{\,x^4}{4}\right]_{2}^{4} \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _0^1 y^2\left( \dfrac{256}{4} - \dfrac{16}{4}\right) \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _0^1 60y^2 \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] \end{align}

Then, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int _0^1 60y^2\, \textrm dy & = 60 \left[\dfrac{y^3}{3}\right]_0^1 \\[5pt] & = 60\cdot\dfrac13 \\[5pt] & = 20 \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} 9x^2y^2 \, \textrm d A,$ where $D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:1 \leq x \leq 2, \: -2 \leq y \leq -1\right\}.$
question.explanation:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

\begin{align} \iint \limits_{D} 9x^2y^2\, \textrm d A & = \int _{-2}^{-1} \left[\int_{1}^{2} 9x^2y^2\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy \end{align}

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int_{-2}^{-1} \left[\int_{1}^{2} 9x^2y^2\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy & = \int_{-2}^{-1} 9y^2 \left[\int_{1}^{2} x^2\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy\\[5pt] & = \int_{-2}^{-1} 9y^2\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3} \right]_{1}^{2} \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{-2}^{-1} 9y^2\left(\dfrac{2^3}{3}-\dfrac{{1^3}}{3}\right)\, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{-2}^{-1} 9y^2\cdot \dfrac{7}{3}\, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{-2}^{-1} 21y^2 \, \textrm dy \end{align}

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int_{-2}^{-1} 21y^2 \, \textrm dy & = 21\left[\dfrac{y^3}{3} \right]_{-2}^{-1}\\[5pt] & =21\left(\dfrac{(-1)^3}{3} - \dfrac{(-2)^3}{3}\right)\\[5pt] & = 49 \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac yx \, \textrm d A,$ where $D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:1 \leq x \leq e,\: 0 \leq y \leq 2\right\}.$
question.explanation:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

\begin{align} \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac yx\, \textrm d A & = \int _{0}^2 \left[\int_{1}^{\large e} \dfrac yx\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy \end{align}

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int _{0}^2 \left[\int_{1}^{\large e} \dfrac yx\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy & =\int _{0}^2 y\left[\int_{1}^{\large e} \dfrac 1 x\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^2 y\Big[\ln(x) \Big]_{1}^{\large e} \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _{0}^2 y\left(\ln(e)- \ln(1)\right)\, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^2 y\, \textrm dy \end{align}

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int_{0}^2 y\, \textrm dy & = \left[\dfrac { y^2}2\right]_{0}^2\\[5pt] & =\dfrac {2^2}2 - \dfrac {0^2}2 \\[5pt] & =2 \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} xy \, \textrm d A,$ where $D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:0 \leq x \leq 1,\: 0 \leq y \leq 1\right\}.$
question.explanation:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

\begin{align} \iint \limits_{D} xy\, \textrm d A & = \int _{0}^1 \left[\int_{0}^1 xy\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy \end{align}

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int _{0}^1 \left[\int_{0}^1 xy\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy & =\int _{0}^1 y\left[\int_{0}^1 x\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^1 y\left[\dfrac{x^2}2 \right]_{0}^{1} \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _{0}^1 y\left(\dfrac{1^2}2 - \dfrac{0^2}2 \right)\, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^1 \dfrac y2\, \textrm dy \end{align}

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int_{0}^1 \dfrac y2\, \textrm dy & = \left[\dfrac { y^2}4\right]_{0}^1\\[5pt] & =\dfrac {1^2}4 - \dfrac {0^2}2 \\[5pt] & =\dfrac14 \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac{y^2}{x} \, \textrm d A,$ where $D=\big\{ (x,y) \: : \:e^2 \leq x \leq e^4, \: 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt[3]{6}\big\}.$
question.explanation:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

\begin{align} \iint \limits_{D} \dfrac{y^2}{x}\, \textrm d A & = \int _{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} \left[\int_{e^2}^{e^4} \dfrac{y^2}{x}\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy \end{align}

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} \left[\int_{e^2}^{e^4} \dfrac{y^2}{x}\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy & = \int_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} y^2\left[\int_{e^2}^{e^4} \dfrac{1}{x}\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy\\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} y^2\Big[\ln{x} \Big]_{e^2}^{e^4} \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} y^2\left(\ln{e^4}-\ln{e^2}\right)\, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} y^2 \cdot 2 \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} 2y^2 \, \textrm dy \end{align}

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} 2y^2\, \textrm dy & = \dfrac{2}{3}\Big[y^3\Big]_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{6}} \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{2}{3}\left((\sqrt[3]{6})^3 - 0^3\right)\\[5pt] & = 4 \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the double integral $\displaystyle \iint \limits_{D} \cos(x+y) \, \textrm d A,$ where $D=\left\{ (x,y) \: : \:0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}{4},\: 0 \leq y \leq \pi\right\}.$
question.explanation:
First, we express our double integral as a repeated integral:

\begin{align} \iint \limits_{D} \cos(x+y)\, \textrm d A & = \int _{0}^{\pi} \left[\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \cos(x+y)\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy \end{align}

Now, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

Making a substitution $x+y=u,$ $\textrm dx = \textrm du,$ we get.

\begin{align} \int _{0}^{\pi} \left[\int_{0}^{\pi/4} \cos(x+y)\, \textrm d x\right] \textrm dy &= \int _{0}^{\pi} \left[\int_{y}^{y+\pi/4} \cos u\, \textrm d u\right] \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int_{0}^{\pi} \big[\sin u \big]_{y}^{y+\pi/4} \, \textrm dy \\[5pt] & = \int _{0}^{\pi} \left[\sin\left(y+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)- \sin y\right]\, \textrm dy \end{align}

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int_{0}^{\pi} \left[\sin \left(y+\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)- \sin{y}\right] \textrm dy & =\left[\cos{y} - \cos\left(y +\dfrac{\pi}{4} \right) \right]_{0}^{\pi}\\[5pt] & =\left(\cos\left(\pi \right) - \cos\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{4} \right) \right) - \left(\cos{0} - \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right) \right) \\[5pt] & =\left(-1 + \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right) - \left(1 - \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \right)\\[5pt] &= \sqrt{2}-2 \end{align}

question.text:
Which of the following equalities are true given that $ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: -2 \leq x \leq 2, \: -1 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}. $

  1. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,\text{d}A = \int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-2}^{2} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \, \text{d}y \, \text{d}x$
  2. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \,\text{d}A = \int_{-1}^{1} \int_{-2}^{2}\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \, \text{d}x \, \text{d}y$
  3. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D}\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,\text{d}A = \int_{-2}^{2} \int_{-1}^{1} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \, \text{d}y \, \text{d}x$
question.explanation:
We notice that:

  • the limits for the variable $x$ are from ${\color{blue}-2}$ to ${\color{blue}2}$, and

  • the limits for the variable $y$ are from ${\color{red}-1}$ to ${\color{red}-1}.$

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{D} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \,\text{d}A &= \int_{\color{red}-1}^{\color{red}1} \left[ \int_{\color{blue}-2}^{\color{blue}2} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \,\text{d}{\color{blue}x} \right] \text{d}{\color{red}y}. \end{align*}

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

\[ \iint\limits_{D} \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \,\text{d}A = \int_{\color{blue}-2}^{\color{blue}2} \left[ \int_{\color{red}-1}^{\color{red}1} \sqrt{x^2+y^2}\,\text{d}{\color{red}y} \right] \text{d}{\color{blue}x} . \]

So, the correct answer is "II and III only".

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $y$, treating $x$ as a constant:

\begin{align} \int_{1}^{5} \left[ \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{5^y}{x} \, \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x & =\int_{1}^{5} \dfrac{1}{x}\left[ \int_{0}^{1} 5^y \, \textrm{d}y \right] \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & =\int_{1}^{5} \dfrac{1}{x}\left[ \dfrac{5^y}{\ln{5}}\right]_{0}^{1} \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] & =\int_{1}^{5} \dfrac{1}{x}\left(\dfrac{5^1 - 5^0}{\ln{5}}\right) \textrm dx \\[5pt] & =\int_{1}^{5} \dfrac{1}{x}\left(\dfrac{4}{\ln{5}}\right) \, \textrm dx \\[5pt] & =\int_{1}^{5} \dfrac{4}{\ln{5}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm dx \end{align}

Then, we integrate with respect to $x\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align} \int_{1}^{5} \dfrac{4}{\ln{5}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{x} \, \textrm dx & =\dfrac{4}{\ln{5}} \Big[\ln{x}\Big]_1^5 \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{4}{\ln{5}}\left(\ln{5} - \ln{1}\right) \\[5pt] & = 4 \end{align}

question.text:
Which of the following equalities are true given that $ D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq x \leq \sqrt{2}, \: 0 \leq y \leq 1 \big\}. $

  1. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{1} \int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \text{d}x \, \text{d}y$
  2. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \,\text{d}A= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \text{d}y\, \text{d}x$
  3. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \,\text{d}A = \int_{1}^{\sqrt{2}} \int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \text{d}y \, \text{d}x$
question.explanation:
We notice that:

  • the limits for the variable $x$ are from ${\color{blue}1}$ to ${\color{blue}\sqrt{2}}$, and

  • the limits for the variable $y$ are from ${\color{red}0}$ to ${\color{red}1}.$

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \,\text{d}A &= \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{red}1} \left[ \int_{\color{blue}1}^{\color{blue}\sqrt{2}} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \,\text{d}{\color{blue}x} \right] \text{d}{\color{red}y}. \end{align*}

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

\[ \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \,\text{d}A = \int_{\color{blue}1}^{\color{blue}\sqrt{2}} \left[ \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{red}1} \dfrac{x}{y^2+1} \,\text{d}{\color{red}y} \right] \text{d}{\color{blue}x} . \]

So, the correct answer is "I and III only".

question.text:
Which of the following equalities are true given that $ D = \bigg\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}2, \: 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}4 \bigg\}. $

  1. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2}\,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \text{d}y\, \text{d}x$$\quad$
  2. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \text{d}x \, \text{d}y$
  3. $\displaystyle \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \,\text{d}A = \int_{0}^{\pi/4} \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \text{d}x \, \text{d}y$
question.explanation:
We notice that:

  • the limits for the variable $x$ are from ${\color{blue}0}$ to ${\color{blue}\dfrac{\pi}2}$, and

  • the limits for the variable $y$ are from ${\color{red}0}$ to ${\color{red}\dfrac{\pi}4}.$

Therefore,

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_{D} \ \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \,\text{d}A &= \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{red}\pi/4} \left[ \int_{\color{blue}0}^{\color{blue}{\pi/2}} \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \,\text{d}{\color{blue}x} \right] \text{d}{\color{red}y}. \end{align*}

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

\[ \iint\limits_{D} \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \,\text{d}A = \int_{\color{blue}0}^{\color{blue}{\pi/2}} \left[ \int_{\color{red}0}^{\color{red}\pi/4} \dfrac{\sin(2y)}{\cos(x)+2} \,\text{d}{\color{red}y} \right] \text{d}{\color{blue}x} . \]

So, the correct answer is "I and III only".
